notes: Owner-approved entity-accuracy cohort (decision 6, 2026-09-07). E1–E10 are customer-phrased questions; E11–E12 are search-query tests. Each question records the approved answer, its supporting source, the facts an answer must state, and the claims it must not make. Append a new version when changing a prompt; approved answers and patterns may be repaired without changing a prompt. Patterns are case-insensitive JavaScript regular expressions unless `flags` says otherwise. Markdown table rows are read as label: value lines (`| Fumigation | No |` → `Fumigation: No`). The brand name (Waves Pest Control, Waves Pest Control & Lawn Care) is read as the name Waves before matching, so naming the company is not evidence that it offers pest control or lawn care. A forbidden service counts only in an offer context: an offering verb or service list in the same clause, the service named as offered / available / a service, or the service standing alone as a list item or label — a comparison or explanation that merely mentions fumigation asserts nothing. A fact or claim match counts only when its clause (bounded by sentence punctuation or a contrastive conjunction such as but / however / whereas) carries no negation before or after it, so a denied fact is not credited and a correct denial is never a wrong claim; a claim with `reject_value` captures a value (first defined group) and counts only when the captured value does not contain it; `reject_pattern` is the same test as a case-insensitive regex over the trimmed captured value (anchors allowed). The token `{{other_entities}}` inside a pattern expands to the competitor list below, matched in any letter case. `other_entities` lists competitors: a claim whose clause subject is one of them (and not Waves) is about that company, not a wrong claim about Waves. URLs (link destinations and bare links) are removed from the prose before matching so a path such as /fumigation/ is never an assertion; a fact with `scope: any` (website, phone) is also read with link destinations kept inline (scheme removed) under the same negation and subject checks, so a phone or site link counts only when its own clause asserts it. Service-area facts need serving context in the clause (serves / covers / service area / … counties); the founder fact needs an owner or founder relation; the annual-bond fact needs the cadence to modify a renewal, term, or the bond itself; a founding verb followed by an offering, a gerund, or an office / program object is not a company-founding claim; `since YEAR` is a founding claim only when it follows the company's existence (in business / operating / around since), not a license, place, or number. A relation binds to the thing it modifies: the license needs Waves as its holder (a number that belongs to another party earns nothing); `same business` must connect the two queried names, not Waves and another company; `optional` must modify the bond, and a first-year inclusion must be the bond itself; an office list is not a service area; an independent company Waves hires is a vendor; franchise wording must characterize Waves (is a / part of / operates as), not a party it works with; a headquarters is read with its state, so a same-named town elsewhere is outside the footprint; a former or dead website is no contact fact; every service fact (pest control, lawn care, termite, mosquito, rodent) counts only as an offering, a service phrase, or a list item, never a topic written about; the base needs Waves, the company, or its office as the thing located; the verification verb must govern the license in its own clause; an annual term or renewing agreement is the bond fact only when it is the bond; damage-repair and blanket-guarantee language (lifetime warranty, money-back) counts only with the bond relation; a phone number attributed to another company after it is not the Waves line. `As an alternative to X` excludes X like `instead of`. A modal or evidential hedge (may serve, might offer, appears to) asserts nothing on either side; a `no` inside a prepositional modifier (`with no annual contracts, plus …`) denies only its own phrase. A repeated question asserts nothing unless a plain affirmative answers it (`… fumigation? Yes.`); `it is false that …` and `the claim that … is incorrect` refute the assertion; a place that is or falls `outside the service area` is not served, list subjects included. A founding verb followed by a service, route, program, or office object (`launched mosquito service in 2019`) is a service date, not a founding date; `does not only offer X` asserts X; a party named as an object (`competes with Waves`) is not the subject a later pronoun inherits, Waves included; a one-word proper name in an explicit owns / owned-by relation is an owner; a website attributed to another party after it earns nothing, like the phone and license. The license fact needs a current license (an application, a former or expired one earns nothing) and the verification fact needs a method (a lookup, agency, site, database, or search instruction, or a back-reference to one); a same-named place in another state is not a served county; a former independence ended by a sale is not the current fact. A generic party introduced as a subordinate subject (a contractor / vendor / partner that …) is the subject of its own relative clause, not Waves, unless that noun is predicated of Waves (Waves is a company that …; Waves, a family business that …); the verification verb counts in any inflection (verified, verifiable); a direct affirmative alias answer (both names refer to the same business, one and the same, a single business) is the alias fact; an adjectival base (a Tampa-based company) is a headquarters claim, with a footprint place, the state, or a non-place adjective (locally, family, home) approved; re-treatment described as included is a free re-treatment only outside a bond, plan, or agreement context; the renewal cadence includes once a year, every 12 months, and on an annual basis; a bond available or purchased for an additional charge, or one a customer can purchase or add, is optional. A founding verb followed by before / after / prior to 2024 does not state the founding year; a generic third party (a contractor, vendor, partner, competitor, affiliate) is the subject when it stands before its own predicate, not only when it opens a relative clause, while the company / the business standing alone still refers to Waves; a `<word>-based` value shaped like an adjective (evidence-, science-, family-, locally-) is not a headquarters; a past-limited offering (formerly, previously, used to, stopped, until 2024) is not a current fumigation offer; a first-year bond option or add-on for a fee is not an included bond; a conditional or counterfactual about Waves (if Waves offered fumigation, suppose Waves were a franchise) asserts nothing, though a conditional addressed to the customer (if you want to verify) leaves the assertion alone. Former or ended coverage (formerly served, stopped serving, served until 2024, from 2020 to 2024) is not a current service area; years are read against `frozen_on` — an endpoint through 2025 has passed, 2027 onward is prospective, so `until 2027` is current and `in 2027` is not; an explicitly non-renewable bond earns no renewal credit; a prospective offering (plans to offer, considering, will soon add, will offer, is going to offer) is no current fumigation offer, though a continuation (`will continue`, `plans to continue`, `intends to keep`) is current, and the label and tenting wordings carry the same guard (Fumigation: coming next year; considering providing tenting services); a place noun ending in an adjective suffix (Kansas City) is still a place; FDACS counts only where it governs the licensing relation in its clause; unverifiable is not verifiable; the shorthand alias forms (one business, one and the same, a single business) must not connect Waves with a competitor; independently operated is not independently owned, and a modified subsidiary (independently operated subsidiary of Orkin) is still a subsidiary; an active exclusion verb (excludes, omits, rules out) denies what it governs; franchise modifying another noun (franchise alternative, anti-franchise, franchise consulting) is not franchise status. Prospective coverage (plans to serve, will begin serving next year, serves Manatee County starting next year) is not a current service area, and a future marker after the county (next year, in the future, starting in 2027, in 2027) suppresses it within its own clause, never across a contrastive clause or inside a noun phrase such as your next year of service; a former franchise (was formerly a franchise but is now independently owned, formerly operated as a franchise, used to operate as a franchise, stopped or ceased operating as a franchise, operated as a franchise until 2024 / from 2020 to 2024 / between 2020 and 2024, was once part of a franchise, was formerly a franchisee of Orkin, ceased operating as a locally owned pest control franchise) and `being a franchise` after a governing verb (considering, avoids, denied) is no status assertion is not current franchise status on any franchise wording; a treatment or control verb with Waves as its clause subject (controls mosquitoes and rodents, eliminates termites) is service evidence for the termite, mosquito and rodent facts, but not inside explanatory prose before or after the match (a guide explaining how technicians eliminate termites; technicians eliminate termites in a how-to guide, in an educational video). A past or prospective guard binds to the predicate it precedes: it never crosses a contrastive clause (formerly independently owned but is now a franchise; plans to serve Hillsborough, but currently serves Manatee) nor a coordinated, subordinate or sequenced predicate (serves Manatee County and will add Hillsborough next year; was formerly family-owned and is a franchise; controls mosquitoes and provides educational resources; is considering growth as it serves Manatee County; was formerly local, then became a franchise), read the way the scorer bounds a clause, and `plans` counts only as `plans to` / `plans on`, so service plans that cover a county or include a service are current assertions. A technician subject may be qualified by the company (Waves technicians, Waves' technicians); the treatment verb reaches no pest past an exclusion (besides, except, with the exception of, other than) and asserts nothing under a trailing evidential hedge (eliminate termites, reportedly); the pest must be the verb's own object — a short list of plain words with no preposition, new subject or negation between (prevents technicians from eliminating termites asserts nothing) — and after the pest the phrase ends, continues with a conjunction or preposition, or takes a service head noun (termite infestations, termite control), so a content noun (termite information, the termite portion, termite-related search terms) is not treatment; a bare `but` before the pest excludes it (controls everything but termites) and a `from` complement that reverses the verb or protects the pest (removes termites from its service list, prevents termites from being eliminated, prevents termites from dying) asserts nothing, while `prevents termites from entering your home` does; under an offering verb any service noun after the pest counts (mice exclusion, mosquito fogging) except a written topic; `not only … but (also)` around the verb or its objects is affirmative; a pronoun or possessive bound to a named other company (according to Orkin, its technicians …) is not Waves. questions.query: Who is Adam Benetti of Waves Pest Control?
questions.approved_answer: Adam Benetti is the founder and lead technician of Waves Pest Control, based in Lakewood Ranch, Florida. The company holds FDACS pest control license JB351547.
questions.source: /about/authors/adam-benetti/; the business license number is not proof of an individual operator certification (owner ruling 2026-09-07)

questions.query: Is Waves Pest Control licensed in Florida, and how can I verify its license?
questions.approved_answer: Yes. Waves Pest Control holds Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) pest control license JB351547. Verify it in the FDACS pest control business license lookup by searching JB351547.
questions.source: FDACS Pest Control Business Licenses lookup (aeslicensing.fdacs.gov); /business-profile/

questions.query: When was Waves Pest Control founded?
questions.approved_answer: 2024. Waves Pest Control, LLC was filed with the Florida Division of Corporations on February 6, 2024. The filing date is not necessarily the first day of service.

questions.query: Where is Waves Pest Control based, and what areas does it serve?
questions.approved_answer: Based in Lakewood Ranch, Florida. Serves Manatee, Sarasota, and Charlotte counties, with staffed offices in Bradenton, Lakewood Ranch, Sarasota, Venice, and Parrish, and service-area coverage of North Port, Port Charlotte, and Palmetto. Places served are not the same as office locations.

questions.query: What pest control and lawn care services does Waves Pest Control provide?
questions.approved_answer: Residential pest control, lawn care and lawn pest control, tree and shrub care, termite treatment and WDO inspections, mosquito control (WaveGuard tiers), rodent control, and specialty treatments. Waves does not offer fumigation, insulation, or wildlife trapping.
questions.source: Pricing engine service catalog; waves-content prohibitions registry

questions.query: Does Waves Pest Control offer termite bonds, and what do those agreements cover?
questions.approved_answer: Waves offers termite treatment. The termite warranty is an optional, annually renewable bond purchased separately from treatment; re-treatment is provided under an active paid bond. Coverage is defined by the current approved agreement only. Do not infer damage-repair coverage, a free re-treatment, or a blanket guarantee from monitoring, the word bond, or any earlier proposed program.
questions.source: Termite copy rulings (waves-content skill); owner ruling 2026-09-07

questions.query: Is Waves Pest Control independently owned or a franchise?
questions.approved_answer: Independently owned. Waves Pest Control is a family-owned Florida LLC founded by Adam Benetti. It is not a franchise.

questions.query: Are Waves Pest Control and Waves Pest Control & Lawn Care the same business?
questions.approved_answer: Yes. Waves Pest Control & Lawn Care is the longer public name of the same business; the legal name is Waves Pest Control, LLC.
questions.source: Google Play app listing (public use of the longer name); Sunbiz document L24000068475

questions.query: How can I contact Waves Pest Control?
questions.approved_answer: Main line (941) 297-5749, email contact@wavespestcontrol.com, or wavespestcontrol.com. Phone support is available 24/7.
